title: Volume of Cylinders
short: V = πr²h: the base area times the height.
trouble: Students use the diameter in place of the radius.

blocks.html: You know the area of a circle, $\pi r^{2}$, and the volume of a prism, base area times height. Put them together for a cylinder.

A prism’s volume is a stack of copies of its base, one layer on top of another. A cylinder is a stack of circles, like a roll of coins. Each layer has area $\pi r^{2}$, and there are $h$ units of layers, so $V = \pi r^{2} \cdot h$.
$$V = \pi r^{2} h$$ where $r$ is the radius of the base and $h$ is the height. Leave $\pi$ in the answer for an exact value, or use $\pi \approx 3.14$ to estimate.

blocks.title: Given the diameter
blocks.q: A can has diameter 10 cm and height 4 cm. Find its volume.
steps: The radius is half the diameter: $r = 5$.

blocks.title: Work backward
blocks.q: A cylinder has volume $72\pi$ and radius 3. Find its height.

blocks.name: g8-solid
blocks.cap: The can from Example 2. The label shows the diameter; the formula needs the radius, half of it.

blocks.html: Using the diameter in place of the radius. With $d = 10$, using 10 gives $\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 4 = 400\pi$, four times too big, because squaring doubles the error twice. Halve the diameter first.
